why: A request whose target cannot be read from syntax is published, never dropped —
dropping it turns an unknown into a false certainty in the direction that makes
the report look better. But not every unresolvable request is an unresolved
ROUTE: a presigned PUT to object storage and an outbound webhook to a customer's
endpoint are requests with no route of ours behind them at all.
So each site is read once and recorded here with what it actually calls. The
generator refuses an entry whose site no longer exists, so a deleted or moved
call cannot leave a stale exemption behind.
OBJECT_STORE          — presigned upload/download against the storage provider.
EXTERNAL_DESTINATION  — an outbound call to a third party or a customer endpoint.
PROP_CALLBACK         — a handler passed as a prop; the path lives where the
handler is defined and is counted there.
LOCAL_NEXT_ROUTE      — a Next.js route handler in the web app, not an API route.
OPERATOR_TOOL         — a script whose target origin is supplied per run.
INTERNAL_API_ROUTE_TABLE — a call to THIS API whose path is picked from a closed
table of literals; the routes are named in consumer-resolutions.
PLATFORM_PERMISSION_API — an OS/runtime API whose method name collides with a
network request is made at all.

const declared = await uploadContinuousSegment(active.session, active.evidenceId, seg) — UC-STR-002 (6934514c, 2026-10-01 review). Inside finalize(), after the bounded queue drains, every segment the recorder produced but the server has not declared (undeclaredSegments(seenRef.current, declaredRef.current)) is retried ONCE from disk; a segment still missing is stated in the manifest as SEGMENT_UPLOAD_LOST, never sealed over. It is the same call as the pump() upload at :175 and reaches the same routes: POST /v1/capture/direct-sessions/:id/parts/:idx/declaration and the part upload (POST /v1/evidence/:id/parts). The path is a runtime capture-session id, so it is not statically resolvable — the reality every direct-capture site has. Reviewed by reading the site.

const result = await PermissionsAndroid.request(permission as never) — UC-AND-003 (6934514c). NOT a network request: `PermissionsAndroid` is React Native's Android runtime-permission API (imported from "react-native" at the top of the file) and `.request` shows the OS permission dialog for android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS, returning GRANTED/DENIED. The analyzer's seed set matches the bare callee name `request`, so the call is modelled as a request whose path argument is the permission string. No route of ours — and no host at all — is reached. Reviewed by reading the site.
